en.g: Trondheim (a city and municipality of Trøndelag, Norway)

1000889.etyen:
From Old Norse Þróndheimr (“Trondheim, Trøndelag”), first part from þrǿndir, þrǿndr (“a person from Trøndelag”) (from the present participle of þróask (“to grow”), from the reflexive form of Proto-Germanic *þrōwōną, thus farmers) + last part from Old Norse heimr (“realm, world, village, home”). Replaced the Danicised name Trondhjem in 1930.
The city was often referred to as kaupangr (“city”) in Old Norse, or more specifically, kaupangr í Þróndheimi (“the city in the district Trøndelag”), which was simplified to just Þróndheimi (“Trondheim, Trøndelag”) during the Middle Ages.

en.g: An inflectional suffix forming the present participle of a verb, broadly corresponding to English -ing
Forming indeclinable adjectives from verbs, often describing an ongoing or characteristic action, behaviour, condition, or effect
Forming or occurring in intensifying adverbs meaning “very”, “extremely” or “completely”, often after the pattern of present participles

1001401.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse -andi (“present-participle ending”), from Proto-Germanic *-andz (“present-participle suffix”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-nt- (“present-participle suffix”). The intensifying adverbial use also continues or was formed after Old Norse formations in -andi, -endi, -indi and -yndi.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -ande, Danish -ende, Swedish -ande and -ende, Icelandic -andi and Faroese -andi (“present-participle suffix”).

en.g: a neighborhood of St. Hanshaugen borough, Oslo, Norway

1004729.etyen:
From the older spelling Bislet. The name belonged originally to a løkke (“enclosed suburban property”), known in the seventeenth century as Bisaalit, on the old road between Gamle Aker Church and Frogner. It probably referred to an inn formerly situated there, but the precise lexical origin is uncertain.
The name was subsequently transferred from the property to the surrounding neighborhood.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Bislett (“neighborhood in Oslo”).
